extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in differential geometry and geometric analysis (readers seeking an overview of Ricci flow)
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedic overview of the Ricci flow: its definition, basic examples, existence/uniqueness, convergence results, singularity analysis, inequalities, and variants (normalized flow, Kähler–Ricci flow, flows with boundary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Ricci flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a smooth manifold M and an open real interval (a,b), a Ricci flow assigns, to each t in the interval (a,b), a Riemannian metric g_t on M such that ∂/∂t g_t = −2 Ric^{g_t}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ricci tensor assigns a symmetric bilinear form on each tangent space so the equation is meaningful; the parameter t is usually called 'time' (informal PDE terminology). The constant −2 is a conventional choice and any nonzero scalar factor could be used after reparametrization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalized Ricci flow
rubrics_metrics.description: For a compact manifold M one can rescale a Ricci flow so each metric has volume 1; the normalized Ricci flow satisfies ∂/∂s G_s = −2 Ric^{G_s} + (2/n)(∫_M R^{G_s} dμ_{G_s} / ∫_M dμ_{G_s}) G_s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The normalized flow is obtained by an explicit change of scale and reparametrization; it is primarily used to state and prove convergence theorems because it prevents trivial volume collapse/expansion. It is not generally meaningful on noncompact manifolds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-time existence and uniqueness (Hamilton 1982)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a smooth closed manifold and g_0 any smooth Riemannian metric on M, then there exists T>0 and a Ricci flow g_t for t∈(0,T) such that g_t → g_0 in C^∞ as t decreases to 0; two such flows with the same initial data agree on their common interval of existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton's proof used the Nash–Moser implicit function theorem; DeTurck later provided a simpler proof using the Banach implicit function theorem. One may take T to be maximal (possibly infinite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-time existence on complete manifolds with bounded curvature (Shi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shi generalized short-time existence to complete (noncompact) manifolds provided the initial metric has bounded curvature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shi's result extends Hamilton's closed-manifold theorem to the complete bounded-curvature setting; bounded curvature and completeness are the key hypotheses for the short-time existence argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence criteria to constant curvature (threefold condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let (M,g_0) be a smooth closed Riemannian manifold. The normalized Ricci flow with initial data g_0 exists for all positive time and converges smoothly to a metric of constant curvature provided any one of: (1) M is two-dimensional; (2) M is three-dimensional and g_0 has positive Ricci curvature; (3) dim(M)>3 and the product metric on (M,g_0)×R has positive isotropic curvature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are major convergence theorems with different proofs/techniques: Hamilton for 2D/3D, Huisken and later Brendle/Brendle–Schoen/Böhm–Wilking for higher-dimensional positive curvature/pinching conditions. The three separate conditions reflect distinct geometric hypotheses that guarantee smoothing to constant curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Li–Yau inequality (Hamilton's version) — hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be a smooth manifold and g_t a solution of Ricci flow for t∈(0,T) such that each g_t is complete with bounded curvature and has nonnegative curvature operator. Then Hamilton's Li–Yau inequality holds along any curve γ:[t1,t2]→M (t1,t2⊂(0,T)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inequality gives a differential inequality involving d/dt of the scalar curvature along curves and includes a Ricci-term; it is important for monotonicity properties of scalar curvature and for analyzing singularity formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perelman's Li–Yau inequality (alternative) — hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be a smooth closed n-manifold and g_t a solution of Ricci flow. Consider the backwards heat equation for n-forms and a particular fundamental solution that converges weakly to the Dirac delta as t increases to t_0. Then Perelman's Li–Yau type inequality holds for any curve γ:[t1,t2]→M (subset of (0,T)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perelman's inequality leads to the definition of the reduced length functional and underpins his noncollapsing theorem; the inequality's right-hand terms motivate monotonic quantities used in the Poincaré/geometrization proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ricci soliton definition and gradient shrinking soliton equation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ricci solitons are Ricci flows that change size but not shape up to diffeomorphisms. A gradient shrinking Ricci soliton satisfies Ric^g + Hess^g f = (1/2) g for some smooth f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the cigar soliton (2D), Bryant soliton (3D steady soliton), and many Kähler examples. Perelman showed finite-time singularities in closed 3-manifolds are modeled on complete gradient shrinking Ricci solitons (possibly on different manifolds). Classification results exist in 3D (R^3, S^3, S^2×R up to covers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Einstein metric behaviour under Ricci flow (example/criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (M,g) is Einstein with Ric^g = λ g, then g_t = (1 − 2λ t) g is a Ricci flow with g_0 = g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sign of λ determines behavior: λ>0 gives contraction and finite-time singularity (max t < 1/(2λ)); λ=0 is static (Ricci-flat); λ<0 expands (immortal). On closed manifolds the uniqueness theorem implies this flow is the only flow with that initial data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up (parabolic rescaling) procedure for singularity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a Ricci flow (M,g_t) on [0,T) that develops a singularity at T, pick spacetime points (p_i,t_i) with K_i := |Rm(g_{t_i})|(p_i) → ∞. Define parabolically rescaled metrics g_i(t) = K_i g(t_i + t/K_i) on t∈[−K_i t_i,0]. Under appropriate assumptions (e.g., curvature maximum at p_i up to time t_i), the pointed flows (M,g_i(t),p_i) subsequentially converge smoothly to a limiting ancient Ricci flow (M_∞, g_∞(t), p_∞), a 'singularity model'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blow-up limits are ancient solutions and are used to classify singularity geometries. Note M_∞ need not be diffeomorphic to M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type I vs Type II singularity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A Ricci flow on [0,T) encountering a singularity at time T is Type I if sup_{t<T} (T−t) |Rm| < ∞. Otherwise it is Type II.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blow-up limits of Type I singularities are gradient shrinking Ricci solitons. For Type II it is open whether singularity models must be steady solitons, though all known examples are steady.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of 3D singularity models
rubrics_metrics.description: For 3-dimensional Ricci flow, blowing up at points of maximum curvature yields one of: (1) the shrinking round spherical space form S^3/Γ; (2) the shrinking round cylinder S^2×R; (3) the Bryant soliton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first two arise from Type I singularities, the Bryant soliton from Type II. This classification follows from work of Hamilton, Perelman, and Brendle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known 4D singularity model examples (limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In four dimensions known singularity models include S^3×R, S^2×R^2, the 4D Bryant soliton, compact Einstein manifolds of positive scalar curvature, compact gradient Kähler–Ricci shrinkers, the FIK shrinker, and the BCCD shrinker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four-dimensional singularity possibilities are far more numerous and less well-understood than in three dimensions; the list above are currently known examples rather than a classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ricci flow on manifolds with boundary — existence/convergence under boundary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: For manifolds with boundary, Shen introduced a boundary value problem for manifolds with weakly umbilic boundaries (Second Fundamental Form is a scalar multiple of the metric) and proved that when the initial metric has positive Ricci curvature and the boundary is totally geodesic, the solution converges to a metric of constant positive curvature with totally geodesic boundary. Subsequent results extended this to surfaces and other boundary conditions; short-time existence and uniqueness have been proved for various dynamic boundary problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific boundary geometry hypotheses (weakly umbilic, totally geodesic, convex weakly umbilic, etc.) together with positivity/convexity assumptions on initial metrics are the decisive criteria for existence, uniqueness, and convergence in the boundary setting. Different authors provide variants and generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to diffusion (2D reduction and nonlinearity source)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a 2-manifold any metric in isothermal coordinates can be written ds^2 = exp(2 p(x,y)) (dx^2+dy^2), and the Ricci flow reduces to ∂p/∂t = Δ p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This directly parallels the heat equation ∂u/∂t = Δ u, explaining the diffusion analogy; the nonlinearity in general Ricci flow arises because the Laplace–Beltrami operator depends on the evolving metric (i.e., depends on p). The 2D computation gives intuition for smoothing behavior and limitations on global flattening on compact manifolds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of Kähler condition (Kähler–Ricci flow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kähler metrics remain Kähler under Ricci flow, leading to the specialized Kähler–Ricci flow studied in that category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This invariance restricts the evolution to the Kähler category and justifies a distinct literature and techniques for Kähler–Ricci flow versus general Ricci flow.
